summary: This bill bars the President and HHS Secretary from declaring national emergencies, major disasters, or public health emergencies to impose gun control and amends federal disaster law to prohibit restrictions on possessing, making, selling, or transferring firearms, ammunition, magazines, or accessories.

scores.thoughts: The bill imposes limitations on presidential and HHS declarations of emergencies or disasters specifically to prevent their use for imposing gun control. It does not mention, authorize, appropriate, or cut any government spending. There are no fiscal provisions or implications related to budgets, expenditures, or funding. Thus, it has no bearing on government spending.

The bill is solely about restricting the use of emergency powers for gun control purposes. It contains no provisions related to taxes, tax rates, deductions, or revenue generation. No connection to taxation.

The bill prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from declaring a public health emergency under section 319 of the Public Health Service Act for the purpose of imposing gun control. While this touches on a healthcare-related authority (public health emergencies), the intent and effect are to protect gun rights, not to alter healthcare coverage, funding, delivery, or policy direction toward public/universal vs. private/market-based systems. The relation is tangential and does not engage with healthcare policy.

The bill's core purpose is to protect Second Amendment rights by explicitly prohibiting the President (under National Emergencies Act or Stafford Act) and HHS Secretary (under Public Health Service Act) from declaring emergencies or disasters to impose gun control. It amends the Stafford Act to forbid prohibitions on possession, manufacture, sale, or transfer of arms, ammunition, feeding devices, or accessories during disasters. This directly and strongly opposes stricter gun regulations and protects gun rights, aligning fully with the +1 end of the spectrum. The bill is primarily about this topic.
